# Four places AI already fits [10 min]{.time} {#four-places}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can name the four places AI already fits, the trap in each, and the one question of the three that guards it.

**Have ready.** This deck on the plan slide, and `orient-and-verify`, which you paste into the chat from its slide and also run in your own assistant. Pick one source to open for it.

**Clock.** 0:00 Day One in three lines. 1:30 the four places. 2:30 the traps. 3:30 which question guards it. 5:30 orient: everyone runs the prompt. 7:45 verify, then your own question. 10:00 time.

**Watch for.** "It's only a question" stops being harmless when the answer changes what happens to a patient. A real patient story in the chat: stop kindly, say the privacy line, switch to a card. A recap that runs past two minutes: cut it.

**If asked.** Can I use it for decisions between patients? Orientation, yes; the decision, no. AI drafts. You decide. A literature-grounded tool shows citations: that makes question 2 faster, and opening the source is still your job. My hospital has approved nothing? Practice on these cards; for real patients, no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Ask your institution what is approved.

**Bridge.** "The second place is the one you will meet first: the progress note. Five minutes on doing it right."
:::

Teaching prep: only text you are allowed to share, and an answer key that quotes it. Each place has a safe way in, a trap, and one of the three questions that guards it. Traps next.

## The trap in each, and the question that guards it {#places-traps}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Daily questions]{.node .same style="flex:0 0 10em"} [→]{.op} [A calm tone on a wrong answer; a made-up citation]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Question 2]{.node .teal style="flex:0 0 7.6em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[Progress notes]{.node .same style="flex:0 0 10em"} [→]{.op} [A dropped fact or a changed value, in a smooth draft]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Question 3]{.node .teal style="flex:0 0 7.6em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[Presentations]{.node .same style="flex:0 0 10em"} [→]{.op} [An identifier left on a slide; numbers the tool supplied]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Question 1]{.node .teal style="flex:0 0 7.6em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[Teaching prep]{.node .same style="flex:0 0 10em"} [→]{.op} [Made-up citations; a confident wrong answer key]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Question 2]{.node .teal style="flex:0 0 7.6em"}
:::

[▲ Place, then trap, then the one question that guards it.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:00.** **Say.** "Each place has one trap, and each trap is guarded by one question." Daily questions: the tone is calm whether the answer is right or wrong, and a made-up citation has the shape of a real one; question 2, does it point to something I can verify. Progress notes: a smooth draft that dropped a fact or changed a value; question 3, would I catch it if it were wrong. Presentations: an identifier rides along onto a slide, or the numbers came from the tool and not your source; question 1, could I defend this to a colleague. Teaching prep: made-up citations and a wrong key said with confidence; question 2.

**Do.** No move yet; the vote is next. Keep the order the same each time: place, trap, question.
:::

## Which question guards it? {#guard-it}

::: {.lane .sm}
[A · A drug-interaction answer, read straight into an order]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [2]{.node .teal .fragment style="flex:0 0 3.4em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[B · A note that lists a medicine the patient never took]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [3]{.node .teal .fragment style="flex:0 0 3.4em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[C · A slide with a scan that has a name in the corner]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [1]{.node .teal .fragment style="flex:0 0 3.4em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[D · An answer key that cites a paper nobody opened]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [2]{.node .teal .fragment style="flex:0 0 3.4em"}
:::

[1 · Could I defend this to a colleague?]{.pill} [2 · Does it point to something I can verify?]{.pill .teal} [3 · Would I catch it if it were wrong?]{.pill}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Type four numbers, A to D: the question that guards each.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** **Say.** "I will read four situations. For each one, decide which of the three questions would have stopped it, and type four numbers in order." Then the answers. A, an answer read straight into an order: 2, because nothing was verified. B, a medicine the patient never took: 3, because you only catch it by comparing. C, a scan with a name in the corner: 1, you could not defend that to a colleague; and the privacy line, once: no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. D, an answer key that cites a paper nobody opened: 2.

**Do.** Read A to D aloud, then run the Chat for about a minute. Read out the spread, not names. Click to reveal each answer. A split vote is a good result: say which question fits best, and why.
:::

## Now verify {#orient-verify}

::: {.lane}
[Draft with AI]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Cross-check the source]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [Confirm or correct]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Use]{.node .dark .grow}
:::

[▲ You have the draft. Read part 2, find one source from part 3, look for the same statement. Not found: it stays unverified.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Your turn: rewrite a question from this week with no patient detail. Type it, and the source where you would confirm the answer.
:::

::: notes
**2:15.** **Say.** "Now the workflow. I read part two, open one source named in part three, and look for the same statement. If I cannot find it, the answer stays unverified and does not change what I do. Your turn: a question from this week, with no patient detail, and the source you would use."

**Do.** Open one named source on the shared screen while the group watches (about 45 seconds). Then the Chat: read out two or three, and point out any that still carry patient detail. Then the bridge.
:::

# Notes, done right [5 min]{.time} {#notes-done-right}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can run a 60-second review on an AI-drafted note and find what was invented, omitted or altered.

**Have ready.** Case A comes from its paste slide, and the draft to review is on the slide, marked illustrative. A timer you can see.

**Clock.** 0:00 three habits. 0:30 the two passes. 1:20 the source: Case A. 1:50 find the three problems. 3:40 what the passes find. 5:00 time.

**Watch for.** Finding all three quickly feels like mastery; there is no announced count in clinic, so say so. Reviewing against your memory of the visit instead of the facts you wrote down. A fluent note that gets skimmed: the smoother it reads, the faster the eye moves. Asking the tool to redo a flawed note instead of correcting it yourself; a new draft needs a new review.

**If asked.** Doesn't reading every line cancel the time saved? Whether you save time is yours to judge, from Lab One's two drafts; the review is the job either way. Can I try this on my real notes? Not in a consumer AI tool: no patient identifiers, ever; ask your institution which tool is approved. Do I have to record that AI helped? I cannot give legal advice; follow your institution's policy and ask its data protection officer or legal team.

**Bridge.** "That was a note written by prompting a chat assistant. In some Saudi clinics the prompt disappears: the tool listens to the consultation. Ten minutes on that."
:::

## Notes, done right {#notes-right}

::: {.lane}
[A fixed template, every time]{.node .same .grow} [+]{.op} [An explicit length limit]{.node .same .grow} [+]{.op} [You read every line]{.node .change .grow}
:::

[▲ Two habits belong to the prompt. The third is the safety step, and it is yours.]{.pointer}

A saved note is trusted, copied forward and read by the next doctor.

::: notes
**0:30.** **Say.** "A saved note gets trusted, copied forward and read by the next doctor, so a mistake in it outlives a mistake in a chat window. Day One's template test gave you the first two habits: a fixed template, so a gap shows, and a length limit, so padding has nowhere to go. They shape the output. The third habit is the safety step, and it is yours. With a real patient the note stays in an approved tool: no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop."

**Do.** No move; half a minute.
:::

## The 60-second review {#sixty-second-review}

::: {.lane}
[Your facts]{.node .same .fixed} [→]{.op} [The draft]{.node .out .fixed} [Pass 1 · 30 sec. Tick each fact off. Can't tick it: **omitted**]{.node .grow}
:::
::: {.lane}
[The draft]{.node .out .fixed} [→]{.op} [Your facts]{.node .same .fixed} [Pass 2 · 30 sec. Find each line. Not there: **invented**. A different value: **altered**]{.node .grow}
:::

[▲ Always against the facts you wrote down, never your memory of the visit.]{.pointer}

**Check first:** [Numbers and units]{.pill} [Medicines]{.pill} [Allergies]{.pill} [Negations]{.pill} [Dates]{.pill} [Side]{.pill} [The plan]{.pill}

::: notes
**0:50.** **Say.** "Two passes of thirty seconds, always against the facts you wrote down, never against your memory of the visit. Pass one, source to draft: tick each fact of your source off in the draft; whatever you cannot tick was omitted. Pass two, draft to source: find each line of the draft in your source; a line you cannot find was invented, and a line with a different value was altered. Spend the time where a slip costs most: 'no chest pain' must never become 'chest pain'. A smooth note is not a correct note."

**Do.** No move yet; the next two slides put both passes to work.
:::

## Find the three problems {#find-three}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
::: {.small}
> **Subjective:** 52 M, hypertension diagnosed 2 months ago, on amlodipine 5 mg once daily for 6 weeks. Headaches (mostly mornings) less frequent. New ankle swelling by evening since starting amlodipine. Missed 2 doses in 6 weeks (forgot while travelling). Home BP diary, last 2 weeks, mornings: average 164/92. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no visual symptoms, no palpitations. Non-smoker. Walks about 15 min most days. Eats a lot of canned and salted food. Father had a stroke at 68. No known drug allergies.
:::
:::

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
::: {.small}
> **Objective:** BP 148/94, repeat 146/92 (seated, left arm). HR 76 regular. Weight 91 kg, height 176 cm, BMI 29.4. Trace bilateral ankle edema. Heart sounds normal. Chest clear. Baseline labs 2 months ago: creatinine 82 µmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.6 mmol/L, urine ACR normal.
>
> **Assessment:** [MISSING: assessment not given in the facts]
>
> **Plan:** Add losartan 50 mg once daily. Keep amlodipine 5 mg. Reduce salt. Keep the home BP diary. Advise walking 30 minutes daily. Review in 4 weeks.
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Two passes, 30 sec each. Type what you found, and its kind.
:::

::: notes
**1:50.** **Say.** "This draft was written for the course, not by any tool. It has three ordinary problems, one of each kind, and I will not say which. The card is in the chat. Thirty seconds for pass one, source to draft. Thirty seconds for pass two, draft to source. Then type what you found, and the word for it."

**Do.** Leave the draft on the shared screen. Say "start" and, at thirty seconds, "switch". Read out the first three finds from the chat without confirming them yet. If fewer than three turn up, say so and go on; the next slide has them.
:::

## What the two passes find {#three-finds}

::: {.lane .sm}
[The card says 146/92]{.node .same .grow} [≠]{.op} [The draft says 164/92]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Altered]{.node .out style="flex:0 0 6.8em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[The card: repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks]{.node .same .grow} [≠]{.op} [The draft's plan: not there]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Omitted]{.node .out style="flex:0 0 6.8em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[The card: not there]{.node .ghost .grow} [≠]{.op} [The draft: "Advise walking 30 minutes daily"]{.node .red .grow} [→]{.op} [Invented]{.node .out style="flex:0 0 6.8em"}
:::

[▲ In clinic nobody announces the count. Run both passes every time.]{.pointer}

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}

::: {.small .muted}
The MISSING line under Assessment is not a fourth problem: the card gives none, so you write it.
:::

::: notes
**1:20.** **Say.** "Draft to source: the home diary average reads 164/92 and the card says 146/92. Altered. Source to draft: the plan leaves out the repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks. Omitted. Draft to source again: 'Advise walking 30 minutes daily' is on no card, because nobody discussed it. Invented. The MISSING line under Assessment is not a fourth problem: the card gives no assessment, so that is the template working, and you write it. You found these because I said there were three. In clinic nobody tells you, so the two passes are the same every time. Correct the note yourself; a new draft needs a new review."

**Do.** Name the kind each time you confirm a find from the chat. Credit a find nobody was sure of: the point is the method, not the speed.
:::

# Already live in Saudi clinics [10 min]{.time} {#saudi-scribes}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can say what an ambient scribe is, read the Sahl AI numbers correctly, and list what to ask before a clinic adopts one.

**Have ready.** The two source links are on the last slide; paste them in the chat at the end. Check each tool's current status and read the Sahl AI abstract yourself before class; everything here is as of September 2026.

**Clock.** 0:00 what a scribe is. 1:15 two examples. 2:45 reading the numbers. 4:00 what the pilot supports. 5:45 six questions. 8:15 the phone app. 10:00 time.

**Watch for.** The title says live, so say piloted for Sahl AI and announced for Augnito; neither source says routine use. The score turned into a percentage: it is a rating scale. Any claim that scribes are better than prompting: nobody compared them.

**If asked.** Is a scribe legal in my clinic? I cannot give legal advice: the PDPL, enforced by SDAIA, treats health data as sensitive personal data; ask your institution's data protection officer or legal team. Which is better, Sahl AI or Augnito? The sources behind this course do not compare them. Where can I read the pilot? Its link is on the last slide; its abstract describes a single-arm pilot.

**Bridge.** "Whether the note comes from a prompt or a scribe, one clinical event still has to be told three ways: to the chart, to the patient, and to the colleague who takes over. That is the next 15 minutes."
:::

## What an ambient scribe is {#what-is-a-scribe}

An ambient scribe listens to the consultation and drafts the note. You do not dictate, type or write a prompt.

::: {.lane}
[Prompting: you type or paste the facts]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [A chat assistant, chosen by you]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [A note: you read every line]{.node .teal .grow}
:::
::: {.lane}
[Ambient scribe: the consultation itself]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [A tool deployed by an institution]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [A note: you read every line]{.node .teal .grow}
:::

[▲ A different input and a different owner. The same reader of every line: you.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** **Say.** "Notes have a second answer: skip the typing and the prompting, and let a tool listen. An ambient scribe works in the background during the consultation and drafts the note. Set it beside what you did yesterday: a chat assistant needs you to supply the facts, and a scribe takes them from the visit itself. You choose your chat assistant; both examples today sit inside institutions. And in both, the same person reads every line: you."

**Do.** No move; keep it to a minute. If someone asks which tool is better, say the sources do not compare them.
:::

Note the tense: that says what was agreed, not how the tool performs, and no accuracy figures are reported. So I say piloted, and announced. Whether either is in routine use where you work is a question for your institution."

**Do.** No move. The two source links are on the last slide; paste them at the end. Do not compare the two tools; the sources do not.

## Reading the numbers like a clinician {#read-the-numbers}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.card .teal}
[What the pilot reports]{.t}

[42.2 of 45]{.big}

Documentation quality, rated by clinicians (modified PDQI-9).

[4.35 of 5]{.big}

The accuracy rating.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.card .dashed}
[What it does not show]{.t}

A comparison with prompting a chat assistant. Patient outcomes. Perfect accuracy.
:::
:::
:::

[▲ 4.35 of 5 is short of the maximum, so the note is still read line by line.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** **Say.** "Two numbers, one careful reading. 42.2 of 45 is a documentation-quality score on a modified Physician Documentation Quality Instrument, rated by clinicians in a pilot. 4.35 of 5 is the accuracy rating alone. The paper describes a single-arm pilot: there was no comparison group, and patient outcomes were not measured, so neither claim can be made from it. It is a rating scale, so do not turn it into a percentage. And 4.35 of 5 is short of the maximum, which is why the note is still read line by line."

**Do.** No move; the vote is next. Do not say which tool is better.
:::

## What does the pilot support? {#pilot-supports}

::: {.lane .sm}
["Scribes are better than prompting a chat assistant."]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [[]{.chk .no} No: nobody compared them]{.node .red .fragment style="flex:0 0 18em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
["Clinicians rated the notes 42.2 of 45 in a pilot."]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [[]{.chk .on} Yes]{.node .out .fragment style="flex:0 0 18em"}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
["Patients did better."]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [[]{.chk .no} No: outcomes were not measured]{.node .red .fragment style="flex:0 0 18em"}
:::

[▲ A no is not a criticism of the pilot. It names a different study.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} For each statement, type yes or no. For a no, add the evidence it would need.
:::

::: notes
**1:45.** **Say.** "Three statements. Type yes if the pilot supports it, no if it does not, and for a no, the evidence it would need. One: scribes are better than prompting a chat assistant. No: nobody compared them, so the pilot cannot say. Two: clinicians rated the notes 42.2 of 45 in a pilot. Yes, that is what was reported. Three: patients did better. No: outcomes were not measured. A no is not a criticism of the pilot. It names a different study."

**Do.** Read each statement aloud and run the Chat for a minute. Click to reveal each row. Then Speak: ask two people to unmute and say what evidence a no would need, or read two answers from the chat.
:::

## Before your clinic adopts a scribe {#scribe-questions}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Review and errors]{.t}

Who reviews and signs the note? What happens when it makes an error?
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Patients and data]{.t}

How are patients told, and how do they say no? Where are audio and text stored, and who can open them?
:::
::: {.card}
[Language and records]{.t}

Which Arabic dialects, and what about a switch to English? How does it connect to our record system?
:::
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Type the two questions you would ask first, and who at your institution could answer them.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** **Say.** "Six questions for the vendor and for your institution; they are questions, not legal conclusions. Who reviews and signs the note before it enters the record, and what happens on an error. How patients are told and how they say no; where the audio and text are stored, for how long, and who can open them. Which Arabic dialects, what happens when the visit moves between Arabic and English, and how it connects to your record system. Health data is sensitive personal data under Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law, which SDAIA enforces. For what that means for your clinic, ask your institution's data protection officer or legal team. This is education, not legal advice."

**Do.** Run the Chat and read out three answers, with who each person would ask. If someone asks whether a scribe is legal, say you cannot give legal advice and point to the same two people.
:::

## The privacy line
No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop.

**1:45.** **Say.** "One more tool you may already have: a free transcription app on your own phone. It turns speech into text. It is a consumer tool, and a recording of a consultation is patient information, so the privacy line applies: no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Try the six questions on an app you downloaded yourself, and notice how many you cannot answer. Day Three returns to exactly this, and the privacy checklist is what to use before any recording goes anywhere."

**Do.** Run the Chat for a minute and read out the spread of numbers, not anyone's app. The privacy checklist link is on the last slide. Then the bridge.
:::

# Same note, three audiences [15 min]{.time} {#three-audiences}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can write a source-of-truth sheet once, draw three outputs from it, and check that the constant facts agree.

**Have ready.** Case E comes from its paste slide. Run all three prompts once in your assistant and save the outputs as a recorded backup, read against the consistency table, so no mismatch is a surprise.

**Clock.** 0:00 one event, three readers. 1:30 Case E. 2:15 write the sheet. 5:00 check the sheet. 7:30 the patient version. 10:30 what changes, what must not. 11:45 check that the three agree. 15:00 time.

**Watch for.** The patient version losing a limit: "if needed", "with food", "maximum 4 g in 24 h". The letter asking the colleague for something that is not on the sheet. A fact fixed inside one output instead of the sheet: the next run brings it back. Time: three live runs will not fit, so the group runs one and you show two.

**If asked.** Why not one prompt that returns all three? You can, but a wrong fact is then hard to trace and has no single place to fix. Isn't the sheet as much work as the note? It is facts only, and Lab Two is where you try it on your own case. Can it write the patient version in Arabic? It can draft; a fluent Arabic reader must check it before it reaches a patient.

**Bridge.** "That was one story for three readers. The next reader is an audience of colleagues: from a case to a slide deck."
:::

## One event, three readers {#three-audiences-flow}

::: {.lane}
[Case E: the morning after a planned gallbladder operation, going home today]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [The sheet: facts only, checked by you]{.node .change .grow}
:::

::: {.fan}
[▼]{.a} [▼]{.a} [▼]{.a}
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .teal}
[Chart note]{.t}

The surgical team, in clinical shorthand. Up to 200 words.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Discharge instructions]{.t}

The patient, in plain language. Up to 250 words.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Colleague letter]{.t}

The community physician, focused. Up to 150 words.
:::
:::

[▲ Only the audience changes. An error in the sheet reaches all three.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:30.** **Say.** "One clinical event, three readers, and only the audience changes. Case E: a woman the morning after a planned laparoscopic gallbladder operation, going home today. The chart note is for the surgical team, in clinical shorthand. The discharge instructions are for the patient, in plain language. The letter is for the community physician: focused, what they must know and do next. On Day One the framework traveled across three jobs and three cases. Today the case stays the same, and the skill is new: checking that the three outputs agree with each other. Three prompts that each start from memory will drift, so all three draw on one checked sheet. A patient told one thing while the letter says another is the failure we guard against."

**Do.** No move; ninety seconds.
:::

## Case E: the one event {#case-e}

::: {.paste-long}
{{< include _paste-case-e.md >}}
:::

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. A fictional patient. The sheet may say only what this card says.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 30 sec]{.tag} Read it. You paste it under the sheet prompt next.
:::

::: notes
**0:45.** **Say.** "This is Case E, a fictional patient, and the only source for this section. Read it now. You will paste it under the sheet prompt, and the sheet may say only what the card says: the operation, how she is today, the medicines and doses, the limits, the follow-up, and the five return-sooner items."

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Give half a minute, then go straight on.
:::

## Write the facts once {#source-of-truth}

::: {.paste-long}
{{< include _paste-source-of-truth-sheet.md >}}
:::

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. A new chat, this prompt, Case E under it.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min]{.tag} Build the sheet. Do not fix anything yet.
:::

::: notes
**2:45.** **Say.** "The sheet is the fix for drift. Three prompts that each start from memory will disagree in small ways. Three prompts that start from one checked sheet can be compared with it. The sheet is facts only, one per line: the procedure, how the patient is today, medicines and doses, activity limits, follow-up, and the return-sooner list. The return-sooner list is yours: you write it, and the tool copies it. If a fact changes, change the sheet and run the prompts again."

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too, then paste Case E under it. Run it on the shared screen while the group runs it on theirs. Say the time left at one minute.
:::

## Check the sheet first {#check-the-sheet}

::: {.lane}
[Case E card]{.node .same .grow} [↔]{.op} [Your sheet]{.node .change .grow}
:::

[▲ Two passes: card to sheet, then sheet to card. Read these twice.]{.pointer}

[]{.chk} The medicines &emsp; []{.chk} The intervals &emsp; []{.chk} The return-sooner list

Fix the sheet itself, never one output.

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} Check your sheet against Case E. Type one line you checked twice, or one you would fix.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** **Say.** "Now the step that matters most. Check the sheet against the Case E card with the two passes from the last section: source to draft, then draft to source. Read the medicines, the intervals and the return-sooner list twice. If something is wrong, fix the sheet itself, by hand. It is the only place a fact is corrected, and from here on every prompt pastes the sheet, not the card. If the sheet is clean, say so: agreement is a result of the check, not a reason to skip it."

**Do.** Check your own sheet against the card on the shared screen. Run the Chat for ninety seconds and read out two or three lines people checked twice. Fix any error live, in the sheet.
:::

## The patient version {#patient-version}

::: {.paste-long}
{{< include _paste-patient-instructions-from-sheet.md >}}
:::

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. A new chat, this prompt, your checked sheet under it.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min]{.tag} Make the patient version. I show the other two.
:::

::: notes
**3:00.** **Say.** "Across the three prompts only two lines change: ROLE and FORMAT. The FACTS block is the same checked sheet each time, and each prompt tells the tool to use every item of your return-sooner list, so it cannot shorten it or add to it. In the letter, the patient's name and file number stay a placeholder that you add yourself, in your own system, after the draft. Time is short, so you run the patient version and I show the other two from a saved run."

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Run it on the shared screen while the group runs it on theirs, with your checked sheet under it. Then show the chart note and the letter from your backup, and say they are a recorded run. Do not read the outputs out.
:::

## What changes, what must not {#consistency-check}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card}
[Changes with the reader]{.t}

Register. Length. Order. Vocabulary: "jaundice" becomes "yellow eyes or skin".
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.card .tint}
[Must not change]{.t}

The procedure and why. Every medicine, dose, interval and maximum. Every number and unit. The follow-up. The return-sooner list: the same five items.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Watch for
The return-sooner list is yours. You write it; the tool only words it.
:::

::: notes
**1:15.** **Say.** "The left card is what should differ between the outputs, and the right card is what may not. The patient version can leave out lab values and most vital signs. It cannot leave out a medicine, an interval or a return-sooner item. And the return-sooner list is a clinical judgment, and it is yours. If you ask a tool to suggest warning signs, it will, plausibly, without knowing this patient. A tool that adds a warning you did not choose has made a clinical decision."

**Do.** No move; read each card slowly. Say the three words once more: invented, omitted, altered.
:::

## Check that all three agree {#check-the-three}

| Constant fact | Chart note | Patient instructions | Colleague letter |
|--------------------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| Return sooner | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |
| Paracetamol | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |
| Follow-up | []{.chk} | []{.chk} | []{.chk} |

::: {.small}
Mark a cell only when that output matches the sheet. Patient instructions: your own run. The other two: my saved run.
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 90 sec]{.tag} With 30 seconds, which row do you check first, and why?
:::

::: notes
**3:15.** **Say.** "Reading each output against the sheet is not enough, because the drift you are hunting is between outputs. So take the constant facts and read each across all three. A word may change; a number, a unit, an interval or a list item may not. A medicine, an interval or a return-sooner item missing from any output is a failure. If an output disagrees with the sheet, the output is wrong: fix it and check again. If the sheet was wrong, fix the sheet and regenerate all three. Agreement is a result, not a reason to skip the check."

**Do.** Chat first; read out two or three rows with their reasons. Then fill the table aloud, return-sooner first: read the row across the three outputs, and everyone types match or mismatch. Three rows are enough; the take-home table has seven constant facts. Everyone copies the table into their notes for Lab Two.
:::
